analysis.one_liner: Bans the manufacture and sale of semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity magazines, while grandfathering existing ones.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 34 cosponsors in January 2019 and was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess semiautomatic assault weapons — covering most AR- and AK-type rifles by name and by features — and magazines holding more than 10 rounds. People who already owned these weapons on the day the bill passed could keep them, but selling or transferring them would require a licensed gun dealer to run a background check. It would also let state and local governments use existing federal grant money to pay people who turn these weapons in through buy-back programs.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people in communities affected by mass shootings, where semiautomatic rifles and high-capacity magazines have been the weapons most often used. The bill's stated aim is to reduce access to these weapons over time by stopping new sales and manufacturing, while letting current owners keep what they have.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess a semiautomatic assault weapon or a large-capacity ammunition feeding device (any magazine holding more than 10 rounds) [S2].
Covers most AR-15 and AK-47 style rifles, semiautomatic pistols, and shotguns by named make and model and by feature lists, plus any combination of parts from which they can be assembled [S3].
Lets state and local governments use existing Byrne Justice Assistance Grant funds to compensate people who surrender these weapons under buy-back programs [S2].
Requires new magazines to carry serial numbers and new weapons to show their date of manufacture, and requires the Attorney General to keep a public record of assault weapons used in crimes [S3].
Requires grandfathered assault weapons to be securely stored or locked so they cannot be accessed by people legally prohibited from owning guns [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Firearms manufacturers and dealers lose a large segment of their market: the most popular semiautomatic rifles and all high-capacity magazines could no longer be made or sold. Current owners could keep their weapons, but could not sell or transfer them without going through a licensed dealer with a background check, and could no longer sell or transfer high-capacity magazines at all.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun makers, dealers, and current owners

drawbacks.text: The ban reaches beyond military-style rifles: the definitions criminalize many common semiautomatic hunting pistols and shotguns based on features like threaded barrels, pistol grips, or detachable magazines, though an extensive appendix exempts hundreds of named hunting and competition models [S3].

Millions of Americans already own the weapons covered by the bill; because existing weapons are grandfathered, the ban only affects future sales and does not remove the large existing supply, which supporters of gun rights say limits any public-safety benefit [S3].

Owners who want to sell a grandfathered weapon or high-capacity magazine bear new burdens — a dealer-run background check and secure-storage requirements — and could face criminal liability if a prohibited person gains access to an unlocked weapon [S3].

Congress allowed the last federal assault-weapons ban (1994–2004) to expire, and studies of that ban have been inconclusive about how much it reduced gun violence, which is the core objection opponents raised to reviving it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill aims at a real public-safety goal — limiting access to the kinds of semiautomatic weapons and high-capacity magazines used in mass shootings — and does so without confiscating anything people already own. The costs fall on the firearms industry, which loses its fastest-growing product lines, and on owners through transfer restrictions and storage requirements. The main honest objection is effectiveness: with existing weapons grandfathered and state laws varying widely, the ban's effect on gun violence would depend heavily on enforcement and would build only over time.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on January 9, 2019, read twice, and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote for the entire two-year Congress.

narrative.text: Senator Dianne Feinstein introduced the Assault Weapons Ban of 2019 in the Senate on January 9, 2019, with 34 cosponsors (33 Democrats and 1 Independent) [S4] [S5].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S5].
The committee took no further action on the bill for the rest of the 116th Congress, which ended January 3, 2021 — no hearing, no markup, no vote, and no floor consideration [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms manufacturers and sellers keep their market for semiautomatic rifles and high-capacity magazines untouched, and current owners face none of the new transfer, storage, or buy-back rules. No one who wanted the ban got any part of it.

for.name: Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it on the Senate floor with introductory remarks.

for.name: Chris Murphy, Richard Blumenthal, Chuck Schumer, Dick Durbin, and 29 other Democrats and Independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, signing on at introduction including Sanders (I-VT), Warren, Booker, Klobuchar, and Harris.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it in committee with no action for two years.

against.name: Senate Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling the Senate floor and committee agenda in the 116th Congress
against.what_they_did: Controlled which bills got committee time and floor votes; the bill never moved past referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 34 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent who caucuses with Democrats, and no Republican signed on; with Republicans holding the Senate majority and the Judiciary chairmanship, the bill never advanced.

industries.note: The bill bans manufacture of the named AR- and AK-type rifles, semiautomatic pistols, shotguns, and all magazines over 10 rounds — the industry's most popular and fastest-growing product lines. Current owners could keep what they have, but the industry could make no replacements for that market.

Dealers lose new sales of covered weapons and magazines, but the bill channels all legal sales and transfers of grandfathered weapons through licensed dealers, who alone could conduct the required background checks and collect the transfer business.
